input: The performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month, and this passage summarises the principal findings. During the logged period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 22 °C, the approach was 3 K, and the range was 6 K. The approach, which is the difference between the temperature of the cooled water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the air, is a particularly important indicator, because it shows how close the tower is operating to the theoretical limit set by the wet-bulb temperature. The range, which is the difference between the temperatures of the water entering and leaving the tower, reflects the heat load that the tower is handling. An approach of 3 K against a mean wet-bulb temperature of 22 °C indicates that the tower was operating close to the limit imposed by the air conditions during the period in question. A natural-draft tower relies on the buoyancy of the warmed air inside the tower to draw fresh air in at the base, rather than on a fan, and its performance is therefore closely tied to the state of the air and to the condition of the fill over which the water is distributed. Taken together, these figures provide a useful picture of the tower's performance under summer conditions. It is worth noting, however, that performance outside the logged month was not measured, and in particular no measurements are available at winter wet-bulb temperatures, so the figures should not be taken as representative of the whole year, and any judgement about how the tower behaves across the full range of seasons would have to rest on measurements that have not been taken.
target: Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 22 °C. The approach was 3 K and the range was 6 K. The approach is the difference between the cooled-water outlet temperature and the wet-bulb temperature; it states how close the tower runs to the limit the wet bulb sets, because no cooling tower cools water below the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air. The range is the difference between the hot-water inlet temperature and the cooled-water outlet temperature; it states the temperature fall the tower gives the circulating water under the heat load of the logged month. An approach of 3 K at a mean wet bulb of 22 °C places the cooled water close to the entering-air limit for that month, and the tower held that approach across the month as logged. A natural-draft tower moves air by buoyancy: air warmed inside the tower rises, and fresh air enters at the base without a fan. The approach therefore depends on the fill, on the distribution of water over the fill, and on the air state, and a change in any of these moves it. The range is set on the water side, by the heat load the process sends to the tower and the rate at which the water circulates. The two figures answer different questions, and neither substitutes for the other. The values are means and period figures for the month; the record as summarised does not state the variation within the month, and no daily or peak figure is given. The figures describe the logged month only. Performance outside the month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, and the approach and range at winter wet-bulb temperatures are not established by this record.
